category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Classically, Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) is defined as a core temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F)
• Requires multiple documented readings
• Core temperature (eardrum or rectal) is preferred for accuracy.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 70-year-old male presents with 4 weeks of fever and a significantly raised ESR. If infection and malignancy are excluded, the most likely underlying diagnoses are [___].
back:
• Temporal arteritis
• Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)
• These are the leading non-infectious causes of PUO in older adults.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: How have the diagnostic criteria for PUO been relaxed from the classic 'one week of hospital investigation' requirement?
back:
• 3 days of inpatient care
• OR 3 outpatient visits
• OR 1 week of intensive ambulatory (outpatient) investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient with a bizarre temperature chart (>41°C) shows no diurnal variation and a normal ESR/CRP. Contrast this presentation with standard systemic infection.
back:
• Likely Factitious Fever
• Lacks temperature-related pulse changes
• Absence of sweating during defervescence
• Patient typically appears clinically well.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the four clinical subsets of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin used to guide differential diagnosis.
back:
1. Classic PUO
2. Nosocomial (healthcare-acquired)
3. Immunodeficient (neutropenic)
4. HIV-related.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: To meet the definition of classic Pyrexia of Unknown Origin, the fever must persist for at least [___] weeks without a clear diagnosis.
back:
• Three weeks
• Allows time for acute self-limiting viral infections to resolve.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A middle-aged traveler returns from South-east Asia with a 3-week history of fever and night sweats. If blood cultures are negative, which fastidious organism and geographical diagnosis should be investigated?
back:
• Salmonella Typhi (Enteric fever)
• Burkholderia pseudomallei (Melioidosis)
• Brucella species.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Describe the diagnostic yield and specific utility of bone marrow biopsy in the evaluation of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• Yield: Approximately 15%
• Detects: Hematological malignancies (lymphoma), disseminated tuberculosis, and Brucellosis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the diagnostic priority for PUO in children/young adults versus older adults.
back:
• Young: High likelihood of infectious causes (abscesses, viral, TB)
• Older: Higher probability of malignancy or connective tissue disorders (vasculitis).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Which diagnostic imaging modalities are considered the standard first-line for investigating occult abscesses or malignancy in PUO?
back:
• Abdominal Ultrasound
• Computerized Tomography (CT) of Thorax and Abdomen
• Echocardiography (to exclude endocarditis).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Classically, Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) is defined as a core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must be persistent for more than three weeks.
• Remains undiagnosed after initial investigations.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 65-year-old male presents with 4 weeks of undiagnosed fever, weight loss, and a markedly raised ESR. In this age group, the most common non-infectious causes of PUO are [___].
back:
• Temporal (Giant Cell) Arteritis.
• Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR).
• Underlying malignancies (e.g., Lymphoma, Solid tumors).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Outline the modified 'Ambulatory' diagnostic criteria for PUO used in modern clinical settings to replace the classical 'one-week hospital stay' requirement.
back:
• 3 days of inpatient investigation.
• 3 outpatient visits.
• 1 week of intensive ambulatory (outpatient) workup.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the presentation of 'Factitious Fever' with true PUO in terms of clinical appearance and laboratory markers.
back:
• Appearance: Patient looks deceptively well despite high temperature.
• Pulse: Lack of temperature-related pulse rate changes.
• Markers: Normal ESR and CRP despite documented fever (>41°C).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the mandatory initial viral screening test required for all adult patients presenting with Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• HIV-1 antigen/antibody test.
• Essential to rule out acute retroviral syndrome or HIV-related opportunistic infections.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: According to the classical definition, the minimum duration of fever required to diagnose PUO is [___] week(s).
back:
• Three weeks.
• This duration differentiates PUO from common self-limiting viral illnesses.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient with prolonged neutropenia (count <500/mm³) develops a fever >38.0°C for 3 days with negative cultures. Categorize this clinical presentation.
back:
• Immunodeficient (Neutropenic) PUO.
• Requires urgent investigation for fungal or fastidious bacterial sources.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the diagnostic utility of Bone Marrow Biopsy in a patient with PUO when initial imaging and blood cultures are inconclusive.
back:
• Yield is approximately 15%.
• Identifies hematological malignancies (Lymphoma).
• Detects disseminated TB, Brucellosis, or Visceral Leishmaniasis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the primary causes of PUO in children/young adults versus older adults.
back:
• Young: Predominantly infectious causes (e.g., TB, Abscesses, EBV).
• Older: Higher proportion of connective tissue diseases (Vasculitis) and Malignancies.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: List the four major clinical subsets used to categorize Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• Classical PUO.
• Nosocomial (Hospital-acquired) PUO.
• Immunodeficient (Neutropenic) PUO.
• HIV-associated PUO.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classic definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Measured on several separate occasions.
• Must persist for a minimum of three weeks.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 40-year-old male presents with a 25-day history of fever (38.6°C). Despite 3 days of inpatient investigation, no cause is found. Identify the clinical classification.
back:
• Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO).
• Meets duration (>3 weeks), temperature (>38°C), and modern investigation (>3 days inpatient) criteria.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the role of 'Source Control' in the management of a patient suspected of having PUO due to an occult infection.
back:
• Definitive diagnosis of localized infection (abscess).
• Drainage or surgical debridement.
• Removal of infected prosthetic material or catheters.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the most likely etiologies of PUO in a 20-year-old traveler versus a 75-year-old sedentary patient.
back:
• Young Traveler: Infections (Malaria, Typhoid, TB, or HIV).
• Elderly Patient: Connective tissue disorders (Temporal arteritis, PMR) or occult Malignancy.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: List the four distinct clinical subsets into which Pyrexia of Unknown Origin is categorized.
back:
• Classic PUO.
• Nosocomial (Health-care associated) PUO.
• Immunodeficient (Neutropenic) PUO.
• HIV-associated PUO.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: According to modern relaxed criteria, the 'investigation' component of PUO can be satisfied by [___] days of inpatient care or three outpatient visits.
back:
• Three days.
• Alternatively: 1 week of intensive ambulatory (outpatient) investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient presents with a bizarre temperature chart showing readings >41°C, but lacks tachycardia and has normal ESR/CRP levels. What is the suspected diagnosis?
back:
• Factitious Fever.
• Clues: Patient looks well, absence of diurnal variation, no sweating during defervescence, and normal inflammatory markers.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Directly how does the diagnostic approach to PUO change when an initial full blood count, cultures, and chest X-ray are negative?
back:
• Repeat detailed history and physical examination.
• Targeted imaging (CT/Ultrasound abdomen).
• Specialized serology (HIV, Ferritin).
• Biopsy of suspicious radiological lesions.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between 'Classic' and 'Nosocomial' PUO based on their diagnostic settings.
back:
• Classic: Community-onset, >3 weeks duration.
• Nosocomial: Hospitalized patient (>48 hours), no infection on admission, 3 days of investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: State the three duration-based criteria for investigation required to define a modern classic PUO case.
back:
• 3 weeks of illness.
• 3 days of inpatient investigation.
• OR 3 outpatient visits.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classical definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a documented core body temperature consistently exceeding [___]°C.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must be measured on multiple separate occasions.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 70-year-old male presents with 4 weeks of fever and weight loss. Physical exam reveals temporal artery tenderness. In this demographic, the most likely non-infectious cause of PUO is [___].
back:
• Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis).
• Often associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica in older adults.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the role of the 'three-day rule' in the modern diagnostic criteria for Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• Allows PUO diagnosis if cause remains elusive after 3 days of intensive in-patient investigation.
• Alternatively: 3 outpatient visits or 1 week of intensive ambulatory workup.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the diagnostic focus of HIV-related PUO with classic PUO in terms of common infectious etiologies.
back:
• HIV-related: Focus on opportunistic infections (CMV, MAC, Pneumocystis, Cryptococcus).
• Classic: Focus on abscesses, Endocarditis, and extrapulmonary TB.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the primary connective tissue disorder considered as a cause of PUO in younger adults, often presenting with a salmon-pink rash and arthralgia.
back:
• Adult-onset Still's Disease.
• A diagnosis of exclusion within the rheumatological PUO category.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The primary screening laboratory test used to distinguish bacterial infection from viral or inflammatory causes in PUO workup is [___].
back:
• Procalcitonin (PCT).
• High levels strongly suggest a bacterial etiology over viral.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A well-appearing patient presents with a bizarre temperature chart (>41°C) and no diurnal variation, yet has a normal ESR and CRP. This suggests [___].
back:
• Factitious Fever.
• Clues: No sweating during defervescence and normal inflammatory markers despite high recorded temp.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the mechanism and diagnostic value of a 'blind' Bone Marrow biopsy in an undiagnosed case of PUO.
back:
• Yields diagnosis in ~15% of cases.
• Identifies hematological malignancy, miliary TB, Brucellosis, or Visceral Leishmaniasis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the management loop of 'Drug Fever' with that of an infectious pyrexia loop.
back:
• Drug Fever: Fever typically resolves within 72 hours of stopping the offending agent.
• Infectious Pyrexia: Requires targeted antimicrobial therapy or source control (e.g., abscess drainage).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: List the five core aetiological categories of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• Infections (~30%).
• Malignancy (~20%).
• Connective tissue disorders (~15%).
• Miscellaneous/Drug reactions (~20%).
• Idiopathic (~15%).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classic definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions for at least three weeks.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Diagnosis must remain elusive after initial investigations.
• Investigations traditionally required one week in-hospital.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 65-year-old male with persistent fever, weight loss, and hip pain displays a positive femoral stretch test. Which deep-seated infectious source should be ruled out?
back:
• Iliopsoas abscess.
• Often associated with IV drug use or vertebral spread.
• Diagnosed via CT/MRI or ultrasound.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the modern relaxation of diagnostic criteria for PUO regarding the minimum duration of investigation now required.
back:
• Three days of inpatient care.
• Three outpatient visits.
• One week of intensive ambulatory (outpatient) investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the primary etiologies of PUO in children versus older adults (>65 years).
back:
• Children: Predominantly infectious causes.
• Older Adults: Malignancy (solid/hematological), connective tissue disorders (GCA/PMR), and tuberculosis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the four specialized subset categories of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO).
back:
• Classic PUO.
• Nosocomial (hospital-acquired) PUO.
• Neutropenic (immunodeficient) PUO.
• HIV-related PUO.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In cases of suspected factitious fever, the patient often appears well despite temperatures >41°C and typically exhibits a normal [___].
back:
• ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate).
• CRP (C-reactive protein).
• Absence of sweating during defervescence.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient presents with PUO after traveling to South-east Asia. Which specific pathogens must be prioritized in the initial culture and antigen workup?
back:
• Salmonella Typhi (Enteric fever).
• Burkholderia pseudomallei (Melioidosis).
• Dengue virus (NS1 antigen detection).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Detail the diagnostic utility and common findings of a bone marrow biopsy in the setting of idiopathic PUO.
back:
• Yield: Approximately 15%.
• Detects: Lymphoma, myelodysplasia, and TB.
• Identifies: Brucellosis, typhoid, and visceral leishmaniasis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the reliability of oral versus rectal temperature measurements in geriatric PUO evaluation.
back:
• Oral: Unreliable in older patients.
• Rectal: More accurate core reading.
• Alternative: Eardrum reflectance (tympanic).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Name the baseline laboratory tests included in the initial assessment of fever without localizing signs.
back:
• FBC with differential and HIV test.
• LFTs, U&Es, and Blood cultures.
• Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, and/or PCT).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classical definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a documented core body temperature of at least [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must persist for more than 3 weeks.
• Diagnosis requires failure to identify a cause after specific investigation periods.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
coreConcept: Etiology of PUO in the Elderly
front: A 72-year-old male presents with a 4-week history of fever (38.4°C), weight loss, and new-onset scalp tenderness. The most likely non-infectious cause of his PUO is [___].
back:
• Temporal (Giant Cell) Arteritis.
• Common in older adults.
• Often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica and high ESR.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the role of the 'three outpatient visits' or 'three days of inpatient care' in the modern diagnostic criteria for PUO.
back:
• Replaces the classic 'one week' of hospital investigation.
• Allows for intensive ambulatory or outpatient workup.
• Ensures fever remains undiagnosed despite focused preliminary tests.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the typical causes of PUO in younger adults with those in the elderly population (>65 years).
back:
• Younger: Mostly infections (TB, abscesses, EBV).
• Elderly: Higher frequency of malignancies (lymphoma) and connective tissue diseases (Temporal arteritis).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the specific diagnostic category for a patient who develops unexplained fever (≥38.0°C) after 48 hours of hospitalization.
back:
• Nosocomial PUO.
• Often related to central lines, catheters, or post-operative abscesses.
• Differs from community-acquired PUO.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: To satisfy the revised criteria for PUO, the fever must remain undiagnosed after [___] of intensive ambulatory investigation.
back:
• One week (7 days).
• Alternative to 3 days of inpatient stay.
• Ensures thorough baseline screening has been completed.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient presents with persistent fever (39.5°C), looks clinically well, and shows no tachycardia or sweating during defervescence. Suspect [___].
back:
• Factitious Fever.
• Clues include bizarre temperature charts and absence of diurnal variation.
• ESR and CRP are typically normal.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: How does the inclusion of HIV-1 status alter the classification of a PUO case?
back:
• Categorized as HIV-associated PUO.
• Requires fever for >4 weeks (outpatient) or >3 days (inpatient).
• Focuses on opportunistic infections (CMV, MAC, PCP).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the investigation yield of Bone Marrow Biopsy and Liver Biopsy in undiagnosed PUO.
back:
• Bone Marrow: Yields ~15%; detects TB, lymphoma, or brucellosis.
• Liver Biopsy: Indicated if biochemical/radiological abnormalities are present; detects granulomatous hepatitis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: List the four mandatory 'Tier 1' investigations for any patient suspected of having Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• Full Blood Count (FBC) with differential.
• ESR/CRP and Blood/Urine Cultures.
• HIV testing and ANA.
• Chest X-ray and Abdominal Ultrasound/CT.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classical definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a persistent core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
* 38.0°C (100.4°F).
* Must be measured on several separate occasions.
* Reflects significant systemic inflammation or infection.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 65-year-old male presents with a 4-week history of 38.5°C fever and new-onset headache. Initial cultures are negative. What is the most likely non-infectious category of PUO to consider in this age group?
back:
* Connective Tissue Disorders.
* Specifically Temporal Arteritis or Polymyalgia Rheumatica.
* Malignancy (Solid tumors or Lymphoma) is the other major differential.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the role of the modern 'ambulatory' diagnostic criterion in redefining the traditional PUO diagnosis.
back:
* Replaces the mandatory 1-week inpatient stay.
* Requires 3 outpatient visits OR 1 week of intensive investigation.
* Recognizes advanced diagnostic speed in modern medicine.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the diagnostic investigation requirements for 'Nosocomial PUO' with 'Classical PUO'.
back:
* Nosocomial: Fever in hospitalized patients not present on admission; 3 days of investigation.
* Classical: Fever for >3 weeks; requires 3 days inpatient or 1 week ambulatory workup.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the minimum duration of fever required before a clinical case meets the formal definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
* 3 weeks.
* This duration filters out common self-limiting viral illnesses (e.g., URTI).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In the diagnostic workup of PUO, the imaging modality used specifically to detect hidden inflammation or malignancy via glucose metabolism is the [___] scan.
back:
* FDG-PET (Fluorodeoxyglucose-Positron Emission Tomography).
* Highly sensitive for identifying vasculitis or selecting biopsy sites.
* Targets metabolic activity in occult lesions.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient with persistent fever for 25 days shows a normal CRP and ESR despite recorded temperatures of 41°C. What clinical phenomenon should be suspected?
back:
* Factitious Fever.
* Clues: Bizarre temperature charts, lack of sweating during defervescence, and absence of diurnal variation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the diagnostic priority for a patient categorized as having 'Neutropenic PUO'.
back:
* Focus on occult fungal infections (Aspergillus, Candida).
* Screen for catheter-related bloodstream infections.
* Evaluate for perianal or hepatobiliary abscesses.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish the typical clinical triggers for the 'Step-2' evaluation of PUO when initial blood cultures and chest X-rays are unremarkable.
back:
* CT Abdomen/Thorax (detects deep abscesses).
* Serology (HIV, Ferritin, LDH).
* Biopsies: Bone marrow or Liver tissue for histology/culture.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Name the three dominant pathological groups that historically account for the majority of identified PUO cases.
back:
* Infections (~30%: TB, abscesses).
* Malignancies (~20%: Lymphoma, Renal cell carcinoma).
* Connective Tissue Disorders (~15%: SLE, Vasculitis).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Pyrexia of unknown origin is classically defined as an elevated core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Occurs on multiple occasions.
• Duration must exceed three weeks without a diagnosis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 45-year-old male presents with a persistent fever of 38.5°C. The biochemical trigger for this thermoregulatory shift in the hypothalamus involves the release of [___].
back:
• Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF).
• These stimulate Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2).
• PGE2 acts on the preoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus to raise the set-point.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the role of modern ambulatory criteria in diagnosing Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO).
back:
• Allows diagnosis after 3 outpatient visits.
• Or after 1 week of intensive ambulatory investigation.
• Alternative to the classic 3-day or 1-week inpatient stay requirement.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A hospitalized patient develops a new fever >38.3°C after 48 hours of admission. Contrast the classification of this fever with a patient presenting from the community with a 4-week undiagnosed fever.
back:
• Hospitalized: Nosocomial PUO (starts after 48h admission).
• Community: Classic PUO (>3 weeks duration).
• Nosocomial requires 3 days of negative investigation; Classic requires 1 week or 3 outpatient visits.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Outline the pharmacological and supportive steps for managing a patient with PUO experiencing drenching sweats and rigors.
back:
• Paracetamol for temperature control.
• Tepid sponging to cool skin.
• Replacement of salt and water lost through sweating.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Under the classic definition of PUO, a diagnosis remains elusive despite [___] of initial investigation in a hospital setting.
back:
• One week.
• Duration of illness must be >3 weeks.
• Must have documented temperatures >38.0°C.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: An 80-year-old female presents with persistent low-grade fever and weight loss. Identify the most common non-infectious etiologies of PUO in this age group.
back:
• Connective tissue disorders (Temporal arteritis, Polymyalgia rheumatica).
• Malignancies (Lymphoma, solid tumors).
• Thromboembolic disease.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Describe the clinical clues that would lead a clinician to suspect 'Factitious Fever' in a patient being investigated for PUO.
back:
• Patient looks surprisingly well.
• Bizarre temperature chart (temp >41°C) with no diurnal variation.
• Absence of sweating during defervescence.
• Normal ESR and CRP despite high fever.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the physiological mechanisms of 'chills' and 'rigors' seen during a febrile loop in PUO.
back:
• Chills: Subjective feeling of being cold.
• Rigors: Uncontrollable shivering via skeletal muscle activity.
• Mechanism: Hypothalamus stimulates muscles to reach a higher thermoregulatory set-point.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the four specific clinical subsets into which Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) is categorized.
back:
• Classic PUO.
• Nosocomial (Health-care associated).
• Immunodeficient (Neutropenic).
• HIV-related.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The standard core temperature threshold required to define a fever as part of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) is [___] or higher on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must be recorded on several separate occasions to differentiate from transient spikes.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
coreConcept: Common Etiology of PUO in Pakistan
front: A 40-year-old male in Pakistan presents with an evening rise of temperature for 4 weeks, weight loss, and night sweats. Initial investigations are inconclusive. What is the most likely infectious cause to exclude first?
back:
• Tuberculosis (TB).
• Extrapulmonary TB is the most common infectious cause of PUO in developing regions like Pakistan.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the modern modification to the 'one week of hospital investigation' requirement in the classic PUO definition.
back:
The definition now allows:
• 3 days of inpatient care, or
• 3 outpatient visits, or
• 1 week of intensive ambulatory investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the diagnostic duration requirements for Classic PUO versus Neutropenic PUO.
back:
• Classic: Fever persisting for >3 weeks.
• Neutropenic: Undiagnosed after 3 days of investigation (including 48 hours of microbiology culture incubation).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Name the most common non-infectious inflammatory cause of PUO in patients over the age of 50 years.
back:
• Temporal Arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis).
• Often associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In the classic definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin, the febrile illness must persist for a minimum duration of [___].
back:
• 3 weeks.
• This duration is required to exclude common self-limiting viral illnesses.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient presents with a temperature of 41.5°C but lacks a matching tachycardia, shows no sweating during defervescence, and has a normal ESR/CRP. Suspect [___].
back:
• Factitious Fever.
• Characterized by engineered temperature recordings or self-injection of contaminants.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: How does the site of acquisition define Nosocomial PUO according to UHS-standard diagnostic criteria?
back:
• Fever ≥38.0°C in a hospitalized patient.
• Not present or incubating on admission.
• Remains undiagnosed after 3 days of appropriate investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish the primary etiologies of PUO found in children from those found in older adults.
back:
• Children: Predominantly infections.
• Older Adults: Higher incidence of malignancies and connective tissue disorders (e.g., vasculitis).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: State the three essential components of Petersdorf and Beeson's classic 1961 definition of PUO.
back:
1. Temperature >38.0°C on several occasions.
2. Duration >3 weeks.
3. Failure to reach diagnosis after 1 week of inpatient investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In the classic definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO), the core body temperature must be documented as exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must be measured on several separate occasions.
• Established threshold to distinguish from low-grade physiological variations.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 45-year-old male presents with intermittent fever of 38.5°C for 25 days. Despite 3 days of inpatient evaluation including blood cultures and imaging, no cause is identified. Identify the diagnostic classification.
back:
• Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO).
• Criteria met: Fever >3 weeks duration.
• Meets the relaxed criteria of 3 days of inpatient investigation without diagnosis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the four modern sub-classifications of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) used to guide clinical diagnostic pathways.
back:
• **Classic PUO:** General population.
• **Nosocomial PUO:** Hospital-acquired (fever after 48h admission).
• **Neutropenic PUO:** Neutrophils <500/µL.
• **HIV-Associated PUO:** Confirmed HIV with prolonged fever.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient is evaluated for fever of 4 weeks' duration. Contrast the 'Classic' versus 'Relaxed' diagnostic criteria regarding the required investigation setting.
back:
• **Classic:** Historically required 1 week of inpatient (hospital) investigation.
• **Relaxed:** 3 days inpatient OR 3 outpatient visits OR 1 week of intensive ambulatory workup.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Outline the essential initial microbiological investigations for a patient suspected of having Classic PUO before progressing to invasive biopsies.
back:
• Serial blood cultures (prolonged incubation).
• Urinalysis and urine culture.
• Sputum/Induced sputum for TB (AFB and Culture).
• HIV screening and local serology (e.g., Malaria/Typhoid).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: To meet the standardized definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin, the patient must have experienced fever for a minimum of [___] weeks.
back:
• 3 weeks (21 days).
• This timeframe excludes most self-limiting viral illnesses.
• Essential for classifying fever as 'prolonged'.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A young female presents with fevers of 41°C. Examination reveals a clinically well patient with a normal ESR and CRP. No sweating is observed during defervescence. Name the likely diagnosis.
back:
• Factitious Fever.
• Clues: Normal inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP).
• Bizarre temperature patterns without corresponding pulse changes or sweating.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Differentiate the most common etiologies of PUO in young adults compared to elderly patients (>65 years) in a clinical setting.
back:
• **Younger Adults:** Infections (TB, occult abscesses) are most common.
• **Elderly:** Connective tissue diseases (Giant Cell Arteritis, Polymyalgia Rheumatica) and Malignancies (Lymphoma/Solid tumors).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between infectious and non-infectious (Autoimmune/Malignancy) causes of PUO using common laboratory biomarkers.
back:
• **Infectious:** High Procalcitonin and Neutrophilia.
• **Autoimmune:** Very high ESR/CRP but often normal Procalcitonin.
• **Malignancy:** High LDH, Ferritin, and anemia of chronic disease.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the core requirement for a diagnosis of Nosocomial Pyrexia of Unknown Origin in an ICU setting.
back:
• Fever >38.0°C.
• Patient hospitalized >24 hours.
• Infection was not present or incubating on admission.
• Remediable after 3 days of investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In the classical definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO), the core body temperature must be documented above [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
* Temperature > 38.0°C (100.4°F)
* Must be recorded on several separate occasions
* Minimum illness duration of 3 weeks

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 72-year-old male presents with 4 weeks of fever, jaw claudication, and a high ESR. After initial negative blood cultures, what is the most likely non-infectious diagnosis?
back:
* Temporal (Giant Cell) Arteritis
* High-yield non-infectious cause of PUO in the elderly
* Often associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the modern diagnostic setting requirements that allow a patient to meet the criteria for Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO).
back:
* Three outpatient visits OR
* Three days of inpatient investigation OR
* One week of intensive ambulatory investigation without a diagnosis

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the primary diagnostic focus in 'Neutropenic PUO' versus 'HIV-associated PUO'.
back:
* Neutropenic: Focus on fungal (Aspergillus/Candida) and Gram-negative bacterial infections.
* HIV-associated: Focus on Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), CMV, and B-cell Lymphoma

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: List the three broad pathological categories that account for approximately 65% of all Pyrexia of Unknown Origin cases.
back:
* Infections (30%)
* Malignancies (20%)
* Connective tissue/Autoimmune disorders (15%)

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The traditional Petersdorf and Beeson definition of PUO required at least [___] of investigation in a hospital setting.
back:
* One week (7 days)
* Requires intensive inpatient workup
* Modern criteria have relaxed this to 3 days

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A young female presents with recurring fever, an evanescent salmon-pink rash, and polyarthritis. Work-up for infection is negative. What is the suspected diagnosis?
back:
* Adult-Onset Still’s Disease (AOSD)
* Common rheumatological cause of PUO in young adults
* Characterized by high ferritin levels and neutrophilia

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: How does the approach to empirical antimicrobial therapy differ in a patient with PUO compared to a patient with suspected acute sepsis?
back:
* PUO: Withhold antibiotics (if stable) to avoid masking cultures/biopsies.
* Sepsis: Immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour (Sepsis Six bundle)

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between 'Nosocomial PUO' and 'Classic PUO' based on the status of the patient at the time of admission.
back:
* Classic: Fever present before admission/community-acquired.
* Nosocomial: Fever develops >48 hours after admission and was not incubating on arrival

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the high-yield 'Miscellaneous' cause of PUO that must be considered in patients taking multiple medications.
back:
* Drug Fever
* Often presents with a 'well-looking' patient despite high fever
* Diagnosed by rapid resolution upon stopping the offending agent

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: According to the classic definition, a diagnosis of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a total fever duration of at least [___] weeks.
back:
• 3 weeks
• Must also include multiple documented temperatures >38.0°C
• Requires failure to reach a diagnosis after 1 week of inpatient investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 24-year-old presents with a 4-week history of high-grade fever, sore throat, and a transient salmon-pink rash. Investigations reveal a high ferritin level and negative cultures. State the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Adult-onset Still's Disease
• A major connective tissue cause of PUO in young adults
• Characterized by arthritis and leucocytosis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the revised diagnostic criteria for investigating PUO in the modern ambulatory/outpatient setting.
back:
• 3 outpatient visits or
• 3 days of intensive in-hospital investigation or
• 1 week of intensive 'ambulatory' investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 70-year-old patient presents with a 1-month history of low-grade fever and a new headache. Contrast the primary suspected etiology in this age group versus a younger adult.
back:
• Elderly: Connective tissue disease (e.g., Temporal Arteritis) or Malignancy
• Younger Adults: Infections or juvenile-type inflammatory conditions
• Undiagnosed fractions are higher in the elderly.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Outline the management step required to confirm a suspected 'Drug Fever' in a patient with PUO.
back:
• Discontinuation of the suspected agent
• Observation for defervescence (resolution of fever)
• Usually occurs within 48-72 hours of stopping the drug.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: For a fever to be classified as PUO, the core body temperature must be documented as greater than [___]°C on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F)
• Measurements should be core (e.g., tympanic or rectal)
• Oral temperatures are considered less reliable in elderly patients.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A hospitalized patient develops a persistent fever (38.4°C) after 72 hours of admission. If the cause remains unknown after 3 days of specific testing, categorize this PUO subtype.
back:
• Nosocomial (Healthcare-associated) PUO
• Criteria: Documented fever in a patient hospitalized >24 hours
• Diagnosis remains elusive after 3 days of investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Describe the clinical 'clues' that would lead a clinician to suspect factitious fever in a patient with persistent pyrexia.
back:
• Patient looks remarkably well despite high fever
• Absence of sweating during defervescence
• Bizarre temperature charts (e.g., >41°C) with normal ESR/CRP.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the diagnostic utility of C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and Procalcitonin (PCT) during the initial workup of PUO.
back:
• CRP: General marker of any inflammation (Connective tissue or infection)
• Procalcitonin: More specific for bacterial infections
• PCT helps differentiate bacterial sepsis from viral or non-infectious causes.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the single most common infectious cause of PUO worldwide, particularly in developing regions.
back:
• Tuberculosis (TB)
• Often presents as extrapulmonary or cryptic miliary TB
• Remains the most frequent infectious etiology globally.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classic definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a documented body temperature exceeding [___]°C on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must be recorded on several separate occasions.
• Documentation is essential to rule out transient or inaccurate readings.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 40-year-old patient reports daily fevers for 25 days. Despite 3 days of intensive inpatient investigations, the etiology remains unclear. Identify the specific medical classification.
back:
• Classical Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO).
• Criteria met: >38°C, >3 weeks duration, and 3 days of negative inpatient workup.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the revised diagnostic investigation criteria required to fulfill the definition of PUO in the modern ambulatory setting.
back:
• 3 outpatient visits OR
• 1 week of intensive 'ambulatory' investigation OR
• 3 days of intensive inpatient care with no diagnosis reached.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the diagnostic requirements of Nosocomial PUO with Neutropenic PUO regarding patient status and duration.
back:
• Nosocomial: Hospitalized patient, fever not present on admission, 3 days of negative investigations.
• Neutropenic: Neutrophil count <500/μL, 3 days of negative investigations including cultures.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the mandatory minimum clinical duration of fever required to diagnose Classical Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• More than 3 weeks.
• This duration is specified to allow common, self-limiting viral infections to resolve before labeling as PUO.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In the context of Classical PUO, the three major etiological categories are Infections, Malignancy, and [___].
back:
• Connective Tissue Disorders (Non-infectious inflammatory diseases).
• Common examples: SLE, Still’s disease, and Temporal Arteritis (especially in elderly).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient with confirmed HIV infection presents with a persistent fever for 5 weeks. State the specific investigation criteria required to label this as HIV-associated PUO.
back:
• Duration: >4 weeks for outpatients (or >3 days for inpatients).
• Investigation: Diagnosis remains uncertain after 3 days of workup including cultures.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Differentiate between Factitious Fever and true PUO based on physiological responses during temperature spikes.
back:
• True PUO: Shows diurnal variation, tachycardia (10bpm per 1°F rise), and sweating during defervescence.
• Factitious: Absence of sweating, normal heart rate, and look surprisingly 'well'.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the primary causes of PUO in younger adults versus elderly patients (age >60).
back:
• Younger: More likely to have infections (TB, abscesses).
• Elderly: Higher incidence of connective tissue disorders (Temporal arteritis/PMR) and solid malignancies.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: What percentage of PUO cases typically remain 'idiopathic' or undiagnosed despite extensive testing?
back:
• Approximately 15%.
• Prognosis: Usually good if significant weight loss and systemic signs are absent.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classic clinical definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a documented core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F)
• Duration must exceed 3 weeks
• Diagnosis remains uncertain after 1 week of hospital investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 45-year-old male presents with a 4-week history of recurrent fever (38.5°C). Initial blood cultures, CXR, and basic labs remain non-diagnostic after 3 days of inpatient evaluation. Identify the clinical classification.
back:
• Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO)
• Meets the >38°C and >3 weeks duration criteria
• Satisfies modern 3-day inpatient investigation requirement.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the investigation requirements for the 'relaxed' modern definition of PUO as compared to the classic 1961 definition.
back:
• Modern: 3 days inpatient OR 3 outpatient visits
• Modern: Alternatively, 1 week of intensive ambulatory investigation
• Classic: Required 1 full week of inpatient study.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 72-year-old patient presents with persistent PUO and weight loss. Contrast the most likely non-infectious inflammatory diagnosis in this age group with the most common infectious cause.
back:
• Inflammatory: Temporal Arteritis/Polymyalgia Rheumatica
• Infectious: Tuberculosis (often extrapulmonary/cryptic miliary)
• Contrast: Elderly have higher malignancy/connective tissue risk than youth.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: List the four specific sub-categories into which modern clinical practice divides Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• Classic PUO
• Nosocomial (Health-care associated)
• Neutropenic (Immunodeficient)
• HIV-associated.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In patients with suspected PUO, the minimum duration of illness required to satisfy the diagnostic criteria is [___] weeks.
back:
• Three (3) weeks
• Shorter durations are classified as 'Fever with localizing signs' or 'Acute self-limiting fever'.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A hospitalized patient develops a fever of 38.4°C on day 5 of admission. If the cause is not found after 3 days of testing, name the specific PUO subset and the priority focus for investigation.
back:
• Subset: Nosocomial PUO
• Focus: Infected hardware (catheters/prosthetics), C. difficile, or pulmonary embolism
• Requirement: Patient was not febrile on admission.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: How is the diagnosis of 'Factitious Fever' confirmed in a patient who appears well despite a 'bizarre' temperature chart (>41°C)?
back:
• Method: Observed/Supervised temperature measurement
• Physiological Clue: Normal ESR/CRP and absence of diurnal variation
• Clinical Clue: Lack of sweating during defervescence.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the primary etiology groups of PUO in younger adults versus those over 65 years of age.
back:
• Younger: Primarily infections (30%)
• Older: Higher proportion of connective tissue disorders (GCA) and solid tumors
• Both: TB remains a significant cause across ages.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the non-microbiological laboratory marker often prioritized in PUO workups to screen for Adult-onset Still’s disease or Hemophagocytic syndrome.
back:
• Serum Ferritin
• Extreme elevations point toward hyper-inflammatory syndromes
• Used as an adjunct when cultures/imaging are negative.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classic definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a documented core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
* 38.0°C (100.4°F).
* Must occur on multiple separate occasions.
* Reflects true fever rather than transient elevation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 70-year-old male presents with persistent fever for 4 weeks and a markedly raised ESR, but initial cultures are negative. Considering his age, which specific inflammatory condition must be ruled out as a cause of PUO?
back:
* Temporal arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis).
* Polymyalgia rheumatica.
* Requires urgent biopsy or imaging to prevent vision loss.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the modern 'relaxed' diagnostic criteria for PUO regarding the setting and duration of investigation.
back:
* Duration: Fever >3 weeks.
* Investigation: 3 days of inpatient care OR 3 outpatient visits OR 1 week of intensive ambulatory workup.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 22-year-old student presents with 4 weeks of fever and weight loss. Contrast the likely primary diagnostic category for this patient against a 65-year-old patient with similar symptoms.
back:
* Younger: Predominantly infectious (Tuberculosis, enteric fevers, or occult abscesses).
* Older: Increased likelihood of malignancies (Lymphoma) or connective tissue disorders (Vasculitis).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: During the workup for PUO, if a patient is on multiple medications, what is the mandatory pharmacological step to exclude 'Drug Fever'?
back:
* Systematic withdrawal of suspected drugs.
* Focus on antibiotics (beta-lactams) and anticonvulsants.
* Fever typically resolves within 72 hours of cessation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In the categorisation of PUO, 'Nosocomial PUO' is diagnosed when a hospitalized patient develops a fever of 38°C+ that was not present on admission and remains undiagnosed after [___] days of investigation.
back:
* Three (3) days.
* Patient must be hospitalized for at least 48 hours.
* Includes negative cultures after 72 hours of incubation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient with persistent fever for 1 month appears clinically well, shows a 'bizarre' temperature chart without diurnal variation, and has a normal ESR. Suggest the underlying cause.
back:
* Factitious Fever (Self-induced).
* Clues: Lack of sweating during defervescence and normal inflammatory markers despite high recorded temperature.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In a Pakistani clinical setting, why is Bone Marrow Aspiration/Biopsy considered a high-yield mechanism for diagnosing PUO when blood cultures are sterile?
back:
* Provides ~15% diagnostic yield.
* Identifies: Disseminated Tuberculosis (granulomas), Hematological malignancies (Lymphoma), and Brucellosis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
coreConcept: Subsets of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin
front: Contrast the diagnostic focus for Neutropenic PUO versus HIV-associated PUO.
back:
* Neutropenic: Focus on fungal infections (Aspergillus, Candida) and Gram-negative sepsis.
* HIV-associated: Focus on MAC, CMV, and Pneumocystis jirovecii.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the most common infectious cause of PUO globally, particularly in developing nations.
back:
* Tuberculosis (TB).
* Frequently presents as extrapulmonary or cryptic miliary disease.
* Often requires tissue biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The standard core body temperature threshold required on multiple occasions to meet the definition of pyrexia of unknown origin is [___] degrees Celsius.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must be recorded on several separate occasions.
• Ensures the fever is clinically significant and not a localized transient rise.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
coreConcept: Connective Tissue Causes of PUO in Elderly
front: A 68-year-old male presents with persistent fever for 4 weeks, weight loss, and a new-onset headache with scalp tenderness. Laboratory tests reveal an ESR of 110 mm/hr. What is the most likely non-infectious diagnosis to exclude?
back:
• Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis).
• A major connective tissue cause of PUO in the elderly.
• Requires urgent biopsy and glucocorticoids to prevent permanent blindness.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha) induce the elevated hypothalamic set-point seen in PUO.
back:
• Cytokines stimulate the synthesis of Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2).
• PGE2 acts on receptors in the preoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
• This shifts the thermoregulatory set-point to a higher level.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 22-year-old medical student has a daily evening fever for 25 days. Physical exam reveals an evanescent salmon-pink rash and polyarthritis. Ferritin levels are markedly elevated (>3000 ng/mL). What is the underlying diagnosis?
back:
• Adult-Onset Still’s Disease (AOSD).
• A classic inflammatory cause of PUO in young adults.
• Typically presents with hyperferritinemia and neutrophilic leukocytosis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: List the three modern 'relaxed' clinical criteria that fulfill the investigation requirement for PUO if a diagnosis is not reached within three weeks of symptoms.
back:
• 3 days of inpatient investigation.
• OR 3 separate outpatient visits.
• OR 1 week of intensive ambulatory (outpatient) investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In the classic Petersdorf and Beeson definition of PUO, the fever must persist for a minimum of [___] weeks to be categorized as such.
back:
• 3 weeks.
• This duration is designed to allow short-lived, self-limiting viral infections to resolve spontaneously.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient with high recorded fevers (40°C) appears clinically well, shows no diurnal temperature variation, and lacks sweating during defervescence. ESR and CRP are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back:
• Factitious Fever.
• Characterized by engineered high readings.
• Discrepancy between high 'fever' and normal inflammatory markers is a key diagnostic clue.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the typical etiology of PUO in younger adults versus older adults (>65 years).
back:
• Younger: More likely to have infectious causes (TB, abscesses) or Still's disease.
• Older: More likely to have non-infectious causes like Temporal Arteritis or Malignancies.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the four standardized clinical subsets used to categorize Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• Classic PUO.
• Nosocomial (Hospital-acquired) PUO.
• Neutropenic (Immunodeficient) PUO.
• HIV-associated PUO.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the most common infectious cause of PUO in developing countries like Pakistan, particularly involving extrapulmonary sites.
back:
• Tuberculosis (TB).
• Extrapulmonary TB or cryptic miliary TB are primary causes.
• Often presents without classic pulmonary findings on initial chest X-ray.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classic diagnostic definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a documented core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must occur on several occasions to exclude transient spikes.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 70-year-old male presents with persistent fever of 4 weeks, high ESR, and jaw claudication. Despite negative blood cultures, this PUO subset suggests [___].
back:
• Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis).
• Common non-infectious PUO cause in elderly.
• Requires urgent temporal artery biopsy and corticosteroids.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Outline the physiological pathway by which pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) induce the febrile response seen in PUO.
back:
• Cytokines stimulate Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) production.
• PGE2 acts on the preoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
• Hypothalamic set-point is raised, triggering heat conservation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient presents with high recorded temperatures but appears surprisingly well, shows no diurnal variation in pulse, and has normal inflammatory markers. Identify the likely condition.
back:
• Factitious Fever.
• Clues: Absence of sweating, normal ESR/CRP, and temperatures >41°C without systemic distress.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: State the specialized clinical categories (subsets) of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin besides the 'Classic' form.
back:
• Nosocomial PUO (Health care-associated).
• Neutropenic PUO (Immunodeficient).
• HIV-associated PUO.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Under modern diagnostic criteria, a fever is classified as PUO if it persists for [___] and remains undiagnosed after 3 days of inpatient care or 3 outpatient visits.
back:
• 3 weeks.
• This duration distinguishes PUO from common self-limiting viral infections.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the investigation requirements between the 'Classic' Petersdorf criteria and the 'Modern' revised definition of PUO.
back:
• Classic: 1 week of inpatient investigation required.
• Modern: 3 days of inpatient care OR 3 outpatient visits OR 1 week of ambulatory workup.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the diagnostic utility of Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-PET/CT scans in a patient with negative initial PUO screens.
back:
• Detects occult metabolic activity (malignancy/inflammation).
• Identifies deep-seated abscesses or large-vessel vasculitis.
• Provides specific targets for diagnostic biopsy.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish the typical etiological profile of PUO in younger adults versus older adults.
back:
• Younger: Mostly infections (TB, abscesses) and Still’s disease.
• Older: Higher rates of Malignancy and Connective Tissue Disorders (GCA, Polymyalgia Rheumatica).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: List the four major diagnostic categories that account for approximately 80-85% of confirmed PUO cases.
back:
• Infections (~30%).
• Malignancy (~20%).
• Connective Tissue/Autoimmune (~15%).
• Miscellaneous/Drugs (~20%).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: In the classic definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO), the minimum temperature threshold required on multiple occasions is [___]°C.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Must be documented on several occasions.
• Classic PUO requires a duration of >3 weeks.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 72-year-old male presents with persistent fever for 4 weeks, localized headache, and a raised ESR. Tenderness is noted over the temple. State the most likely non-infectious etiology.
back:
• Temporal Arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis).
• Common non-infectious cause in the elderly.
• Often associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: How has the diagnostic requirement for 'investigation' changed in the modern definition of PUO compared to the classic 'one week of hospitalization'?
back:
• 3 days of inpatient investigation.
• 3 outpatient visits.
• OR 1 week of intensive ambulatory (outpatient) investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient with PUO shows core temperatures >41°C, a bizarre fever chart with no diurnal variation, and remains well-appearing without sweating during defervescence. Identify the likely classification.
back:
• Factitious Fever.
• Clues: Normal CRP/ESR despite high fever.
• Often involves self-injection or thermometer manipulation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the specific subset of PUO categorized by fever appearing in a patient receiving acute hospital care that was not present or incubating upon admission.
back:
• Nosocomial PUO.
• Requires 3 days of investigation.
• Often related to surgery, catheters, or C. difficile.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: To meet the diagnostic duration criteria for Classic Pyrexia of Unknown Origin, the fever must persist for a minimum of [___] weeks.
back:
• Three weeks.
• Ensures transient viral illnesses are excluded.
• Allows time for initial diagnostic workup.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: An IV drug user presents with persistent fever, new heart murmur, and splinter hemorrhages. Explain the role of echocardiography in this PUO workup.
back:
• Identifies Infective Endocarditis.
• Detects valvular vegetations/abscesses.
• Critical for diagnosing 'Culture-Negative' endocarditis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain why HIV-related PUO is investigated differently than the classic PUO category.
back:
• Unique pathogens: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), CMV, Pneumocystis.
• Different duration: Requires 4 weeks (outpatient) or 3 days (inpatient).
• Driven by CD4 count status.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the primary diagnostic focus for PUO in children versus adults over 50 years of age.
back:
• Children: Predominantly infectious causes (viral/bacterial).
• Older Adults: Higher incidence of Malignancy and Connective Tissue Disorders (Vasculitis).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Name the three broad categories of disease that historically account for approximately 65-70% of identified PUO cases.
back:
• Infections (~30%).
• Malignancy (~20%).
• Connective Tissue/Inflammatory Disorders (~15%).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Classic Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) is defined as a core body temperature exceeding [___] on multiple occasions for more than three weeks.
back:
* 38.0°C (100.4°F)
* Must persist for at least three weeks
* Diagnosis remains uncertain after initial intensive investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 65-year-old male presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, and new-onset headache with scalp tenderness. ESR is 100 mm/hr. The most likely non-infectious cause of his PUO is [___].
back:
* Temporal arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis)
* Key autoimmune cause of PUO in the elderly
* Often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Describe the role of the hypothalamus and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in the generation of fever.
back:
* Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) stimulate PGE2 production
* PGE2 acts on the preoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus
* This resets the thermoregulatory set-point to a higher level.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the primary etiological categories of PUO found in children versus those predominantly found in older adults.
back:
* Children: Mostly infectious causes (viral, TB, or atypical infections)
* Elderly: Higher incidence of malignancies (lymphoma) and connective tissue disorders (Temporal arteritis).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the mandatory initial screening investigations for a patient suspected of having Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
* FBC with differential, ESR, and CRP
* Multiple blood and urine cultures
* LFTs and HIV-1 antigen/antibody test
* Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The revised diagnostic criteria for PUO allow for a diagnosis if the cause remains uncertain despite [___] of inpatient investigation or three outpatient visits.
back:
* Three days
* Relaxed from the classical one-week inpatient requirement
* Includes intensive ambulatory investigation for one week.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient presents with a temperature of 41.5°C but appears clinically well, with a normal ESR and no sweating during defervescence. Identify the likely diagnosis.
back:
* Factitious Fever
* Clues: Lack of diurnal variation and normal inflammatory markers
* Diagnosis is confirmed by supervised (observed) temperature measurement.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the diagnostic utility of a bone marrow biopsy in a patient with PUO and no localising signs.
back:
* Diagnostic yield is approximately 15%
* Most likely to reveal hematological malignancy (lymphoma) or disseminated TB
* Also identifies brucellosis and visceral leishmaniasis.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish between the diagnostic categories of Nosocomial PUO and Neutropenic PUO.
back:
* Nosocomial: Fever in hospitalized patients (48h+); related to surgery, catheters, or C. difficile
* Neutropenic: Fever in patients with neutrophils < 500/mm³; high risk of opportunistic infection.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: State the four traditional major clinical categories into which the causes of PUO are divided.
back:
* Infections (~30%)
* Malignancy (~20%)
* Connective tissue disorders (~15%)
* Miscellaneous/Idiopathic (~35%).

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: The classical definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a core temperature of at least [___] recorded on multiple occasions.
back:
* 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher.
* Must be measured on several separate occasions.
* Traditional criteria required this for over 3 weeks.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A 45-year-old male with a 4-week history of recurrent fever (38.5°C) remains undiagnosed after 3 days of intensive inpatient testing. State the most likely clinical classification.
back:
* Classical Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO).
* Fits modern criteria: >38.0°C, >3 weeks duration, and unexplained after 3 days of inpatient investigation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Explain the role of duration in distinguishing between 'Fever with localizing signs' and 'Classical PUO'.
back:
* Duration: Fever must persist for >3 weeks for Classical PUO.
* Diagnostic Failure: Standard initial investigations must fail to identify a source.
* Focus: Localizing symptoms typically yield diagnoses much faster via targeted testing.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Contrast the diagnostic timeframe requirements for Classical PUO versus Nosocomial (Health-care associated) PUO.
back:
* Classical: >3 weeks duration and 3 days of inpatient (or 3 outpatient) study.
* Nosocomial: Patient hospitalized >24 hours, fever undiagnosed after 3 days of investigation.
* Key difference: Nosocomial lacks the 3-week requirement.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Identify the minimum number of outpatient visits required to meet the modern diagnostic criteria for PUO if the patient is not hospitalized.
back:
* Three (3) outpatient visits.
* Alternatively: One week of intensive ambulatory investigation.
* This reflects the modern shift toward non-hospitalized diagnostic pathways.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Pyrexia of Unknown Origin is categorized into four specific subsets: Classical, Nosocomial, HIV-associated, and [___].
back:
* Neutropenic (or Immunodeficient) PUO.
* Criteria: Neutrophil count <500/µL, fever >38.0°C, undiagnosed after 3 days including 48 hours of culture incubation.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: A patient with confirmed HIV presents with a 5-week history of fever. Initial investigations over 4 days in the ward fail to reveal a source. Classify this condition according to established criteria.
back:
* HIV-associated PUO.
* Requirements: Confirmed HIV positive, fever >4 weeks (outpatient) or >3 days (inpatient), and undiagnosed after targeted investigations.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: How do the common causes of PUO differ between younger adults and patients over 65 years of age?
back:
* Younger: Infections (e.g., TB, abscesses) are the primary drivers (~30-50%).
* Older: Higher incidence of connective tissue diseases (e.g., GCA/PMR) and malignancies.
* Idiopathic: A smaller fraction remains undiagnosed in the elderly compared to the young.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: Distinguish the metabolic/physiological criteria for diagnosing 'Factitious Fever' within the context of a PUO investigation.
back:
* Temperature: Often >41°C with a bizarre chart lacking diurnal variation.
* Physical: Patient looks well; absence of sweating during defervescence.
* Lab findings: Normal ESR and CRP despite high fever recordings.

category: Define pyrexia of unknown origin and state the diagnostic criteria
front: State the standard core temperature threshold (in Celsius) that defines 'fever' in clinical assessment.
back:
* >38.0°C.
* Represents a systemic response to cytokines and acute-phase proteins.
* Core measurement (rectal/tympanic) is more reliable than oral in elderly patients.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: In the classification of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO), the most common group of underlying causes, accounting for approximately 30% of cases, is [___].
back:
* Infections.
* Includes extrapulmonary tuberculosis and occult abscesses.
* Infective endocarditis is a critical specific cause in this category.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
coreConcept: Inflammatory Causes of PUO in the Elderly
front: A 70-year-old male presents with persistent fever, weight loss, and new-onset jaw claudication. This clinical picture belongs to which etiological group of PUO?
back:
* Connective tissue / Inflammatory disorders.
* Specifically suggestive of Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal arteritis).
* Most common inflammatory cause of PUO in patients over age 50.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Explain the clinical clues that suggest 'Factitious Fever' as the cause in a patient presenting with an unconventional PUO chart.
back:
* Discrepancy between high temperature and pulse rate.
* Absence of diurnal variation or sweating during defervescence.
* Normal ESR and C-reactive protein (CRP) despite high recorded fever.
* Rapidly changing, bizarre temperature readings.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Contrast the most likely etiological groups of PUO in children/young adults versus older adults (age >65).
back:
* Young Adults: Predominantly infections (e.g., EBV, CMV) and Still’s disease.
* Older Adults: Higher prevalence of malignancies (e.g., Lymphoma) and vasculitic disorders (e.g., Temporal arteritis).

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Identify the mechanism and appropriate management for 'Drug Fever' within the miscellaneous group of PUO.
back:
* Mechanism: Hypersensitivity reaction or interference with thermoregulatory centers.
* Management: Discontinuation of suspected agents (e.g., beta-lactams, sulfonamides).
* Clinical Outcome: Fever typically resolves within 72 hours of drug cessation.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: The most frequent hematological malignancy presenting as Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) in the neoplastic group is [___].
back:
* Lymphoma (both Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin).
* Often presents with 'B symptoms': fever, night sweats, and weight loss.
* Solid tumors like Renal Cell Carcinoma are also common non-hematological causes.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: A patient presents with 4 weeks of step-ladder fever and relative bradycardia after returning from rural Sindh. Identify the likely etiological category and specific pathogen group.
back:
* Category: Geographically restricted/Travel-related infections.
* Pathogen: Salmonella Typhi (Enteric Fever).
* Common in Pakistan; must be excluded via blood cultures in any long-term fever.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Describe the typical anatomical locations for 'Occult Abscesses' that must be screened for in the infectious group of PUO.
back:
* Hepatobiliary: Liver or gallbladder abscesses.
* Intra-abdominal: Diverticular or subphrenic collections.
* Pelvic: Tubo-ovarian abscesses or prostatic infection.
* Dental: Sinusitis or periapical dental abscesses.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Distinguish between 'Classic PUO' and 'HIV-related PUO' based on chronicity and diagnostic criteria.
back:
* Classic: >38°C, >3 weeks duration, >3 days inpatient investigation.
* HIV-related: >4 weeks outpatient or >3 days inpatient duration in HIV+ patients.
* HIV pathogens: MAC, CMV, and Pneumocystis jirovecii.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Identify the primary connective tissue disorder considered in a young patient presenting with PUO, high ferritin levels, and a salmon-pink rash.
back:
* Adult-Onset Still’s Disease (AOSD).
* Part of the connective tissue/inflammatory group.
* Characterized by high daily spiking fevers, arthritis, and high inflammatory markers.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: The classical definition of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) requires a core temperature exceeding [___] degrees Celsius on multiple occasions.
back:
• 38.0°C (100.4°F).
• Duration: >3 weeks.
• Investigation: >1 week in hospital or 3 outpatient visits.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: A 70-year-old male presents with persistent fever, weight loss, and jaw claudication. Name the most likely non-infectious etiological cause of his PUO.
back:
• Temporal Arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis).
• Common in patients >50 years.
• Often associated with Polymyalgia Rheumatica.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Identify the diagnostic utility of Bone Marrow Biopsy in a patient with undiagnosed PUO.
back:
• Identifies hematological malignancies (Lymphoma/Leukaemia).
• Detects disseminated Tuberculosis.
• Identifies Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar) or Brucellosis.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Contrast the etiological spectrum of PUO in children versus elderly populations.
back:
• Children: Predominantly infectious causes.
• Elderly: Higher incidence of malignancies and Connective Tissue Disorders (TA/PMR).
• Elderly: TB is often a reactivation.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
front: Name the three most common solid tumors that frequently manifest as Pyrexia of Unknown Origin.
back:
• Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC).
• Hepatocellular Carcinoma (Hepatoma).
• Colorectal or Gastric Carcinoma.

category: Classify the major etiological groups of PUO
